title: The Popping Ears
twist: Most people expect the climb to hurt because the plane is going up. It's actually the descent, when the cabin air pushes harder on the eardrum than the air trapped behind it — and a swallow fixes it.
briefing: Lucía, 14, flies to visit her grandmother. Take-off is fine. But twenty minutes before landing her ears feel blocked, voices sound muffled, and one ear starts to hurt. Her little brother, chewing gum the whole way down, doesn't notice a thing.
question: Why do ears hurt coming down — and why does chewing gum help?

clues.title: Fine on the way up
clues.text: During take-off and the climb her ears felt fine, maybe one small pop. Cruising high up was fine too.
clues.shows: that being high up, or climbing, wasn't the problem

clues.title: Blocked on the way down
clues.text: As the plane descends, her ears feel stuffed and voices sound far away. Then one ear starts to ache.
clues.shows: her eardrums being pushed in as the plane comes down

visual.unit: mmHg pressure difference across her eardrum, start → 15 min into descent

clues.title: Brother with gum
clues.text: Her brother chews gum and swallows constantly on the way down. He says his ears are totally fine.

clues.title: A big yawn
clues.text: Lucía does a huge yawn. Her ear goes 'pop' and the ache and muffling vanish instantly.
clues.shows: a small tube opening to let air in and even out the pressure

hypotheses.text: As the plane descends, the air pressure in the cabin rises but the air behind her eardrum stays at the lower pressure, so the eardrum is pushed in — until swallowing or yawning opens a small tube that lets air in to even it out.
The engines are extra loud during landing.
hypotheses.flaw: Engines are loudest at take-off, when her ears were fine — and loudness wouldn't vanish with one yawn.

hypotheses.text: The dry cabin air dried out her ears.
hypotheses.flaw: The air was just as dry at cruising height, and dryness wouldn't be fixed instantly by a yawn.

hypotheses.text: Being high up in the sky makes ears hurt.
hypotheses.flaw: She was fine cruising high up — it started as the plane came down.

prediction.prompt: If Lucía never swallows or yawns, what happens to the pressure difference across her eardrum as the descent goes on?

second.question: If she swallows several times a minute, does the pressure difference go up or down?

concepts.label: a tube opens to even it out

transfer.context: Yusuf, 14, swims down to the bottom of the deep end and his ears start to hurt. When he gently swallows, they pop and feel better.
options: Deeper water pushes harder on his eardrums than the air trapped behind them; swallowing opens the tube and lets air in to even the pressure.
Pool water got into his inner ear.
He swam down too fast and tired his ear muscles.
transfer.retryHint: A pop that fixes it instantly — which of Lucía's clues was that?
transfer.explanation: Going down in water is like a plane descending, only faster: the pressure outside the eardrum rises while the air behind it stays the same. Swallowing opens the small tube from the throat, air flows in, and the pressure evens out — pop.

takeaway: Your eardrum has air on both sides. When the outside pressure rises — a plane coming down, or diving deeper — the eardrum gets pushed in until a swallow or yawn opens a small tube and evens the pressure out.
